newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: SOCCER-JOHANSSON ADMITS STUPIDITY OF RACIST JOKE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JOHANSSON ADMITS STUPIDITY OF RACIST JOKE.

text.p: UEFA president Lennart Johansson said on Tuesday his racists comments were a bad joke but the controversy surrounding them will not deter him from pursuing the FIFA presidency.
Johansson arrived at the UEFA congress meetings following a storm of criticism over racist remarks he made in a Swedish newspaper article where he referred to Africans as blackies.

Having kept a low profile since his comments first appeared last Thursday, Johansson stepped from his car and marched confidently towards waiting cameramen and reporters, appearing eager to explain his remarks.
"In the Swedish papers I was quoted quite properly," said Johansson. "I was using one word which was suppose to be funny and it wasn't funny at all.
"I have no excuse.
"But to turn this into racism is too much for me.
"But if you do something that is foolish and you don't watch your tongue you have to take the result."
Johansson explained the circumstances that led to the remarks, admitting that the interview was taped leaving him no room for denial.
"I talked with journalist I had never met before and he tape recorded it," said Johansson. "You don't know when the interview starts and when it ends."

Until the controversy, Johansson was seen as the most serious challenger to 80-year-old Joao Havelange for the FIFA presidency when the octagenarian Brazilian eventually steps down from the position he has held since 1974. .

The 67-year-old Swede however, may have lost the support of the Africans, who could have helped him swing any future vote for the FIFA presidency, but who are now planning to lodge a protest over the incident.
Asked if he thought his remarks had irrevocably damaged his bid, Johansson said, "he who lives will see, I hope not.
"I will continue to work on it the way I have all the time and in very close co-operation with the Africans," he added.
"I trust with the way I have behaved and with what I have done in the last five years that they will believe me."
With the exception of a brief statement in a UEFA press release, Johansson had done little in the way of damage control until his appearance at the week long meetings.
In an obvious effort to defuse the controversy, Johansson also took the opportunity to apologize for the remarks.
"I will make an apology to all concerned," he said. "I will write letters to all my colleagues to make them understand that this was suppose to be sort of a joke.
"This was a mistake.
"Whether they will forgive or not I will hear.
"I hope they (the Confederation of African Football) will accept my apology because it was not suppose to be connected to racism.

"But when you see it in black and white you regret that you said it." In a separate development UEFA announced on Tuesday that it would be fully supporting the European Union's "Year Against Racism" in 1997.

In a statement UEFA said that two weeks ago the EU made a personal request to Johansson for UEFA's active participation and co-operation in the scheme and Johansson had spontaneously reacted by deciding to associate UEFA activities and events in 1997 with the EU's programmes.
